890.title: The river cut off
890.hook: at Karbala his camp is surrounded and cut off from the Euphrates
890.howItsDone: In Muharram, Shia Muslims remember the thirst of Husayn's camp at Karbala, and some communities set up stalls to offer water and drinks to passersby in memory of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Husayn refuses, a pledge he would not give, and a family setting out toward Kufa. Your line was he would not pledge.

Somewhere on the road to Kufa, the histories say, a troop of horsemen rides up to block Husayn's way. Their commander is al-Hurr. The men have been riding in the heat, and they are parched, and so are their horses. Husayn tells his young men to give them water, and the horses too. The reports say they filled bowls and held them to the horses' mouths, again and again, until each had drunk. These were the soldiers sent to stop him. A few days later, on a plain by the Euphrates called Karbala, the water would run the other way.
screen: `HORSEMEN BLOCK THE ROAD.` → `GIVE THEM WATER.` → `THE HORSES TOO.`

segments.voice: Kufa does not welcome him. Muslim ibn Aqil, the cousin he sent ahead, has been caught and killed, and the city that wrote all those letters has gone quiet under its new governor, Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad. Husayn is turned aside, and his small camp pitches its tents at Karbala, in the open, near the river. Then a much larger army arrives, and the histories report an order from the governor: put yourselves between Husayn and the water; do not let them taste a drop. So soldiers line the riverbank. The Euphrates is close enough to see, and the camp, with its children, its women and its old men, cannot reach it. The reports say Husayn's half-brother al-Abbas led a party down to the river by night and fought his way back with some water skins. Shia Muslims remember al-Abbas with deep love as the one who carried water, and the stories of his last attempt are told with great tenderness in Muharram. The same camp that had watered its enemies' horses on the road is now refused water by men who have more than enough. The Qur'an says that God made every living thing from water; to cut a family off from a river is to cut at life itself. That is one reason water carries this story in Shia remembrance: a glass offered to a stranger during Muharram can be a memory of Karbala. And it is why the plainest line of this story is also the hardest.
screen: `KUFA GOES QUIET.` · `TENTS AT KARBALA.` · `BETWEEN HUSAYN AND THE WATER.` · `AL-ABBAS GOES DOWN BY NIGHT.` · then, large: `THEY WERE THIRSTY.`

segments.voice: If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it, noticing how easy it was to get. Bring to mind the camp at Karbala, near enough to see the river and unable to reach it, then drink slowly, a sip at a time. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you drink and alhamdulillah after; if not, just notice each sip.
Karbala. The plain by the Euphrates where Husayn's camp was cut off from the river, and soldiers stood between a family and the water. Today's word.
Your line: they were thirsty. A glass of water can carry their memory. That's day eight hundred ninety.

891.title: The tenth of Muharram
891.hook: Husayn and his companions and family are killed on the day of Ashura
891.howItsDone: On the tenth of Muharram, Shia Muslims gather to mourn Husayn with elegies and recitations of Karbala; Sunni Muslims honor him too, and Sunni communities keep the Ashura fast that the Prophet kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karbala, a camp within sight of the Euphrates, and soldiers between them and the water. Your line was they were thirsty.

Before Karbala, the tenth day of Muharram already had a name: Ashura. Bukhari records that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, came to Medina, he found the Jews of the city fasting on that day, remembering how God had saved Moses and his people. The Prophet fasted it too, and asked his followers to fast. So it was a day of rescue, kept with a fast. Then came a morning on a plain beside the Euphrates, and the same day gained a second memory, this one of grief.
screen: `ASHURA ALREADY HAD A NAME.` → `A DAY OF RESCUE.` → `THEN A SECOND MEMORY.`

segments.voice: The histories tell the morning slowly, and it is right to tell it plainly. Husayn's small band faces the army. One man rides out from the army's ranks and crosses over: al-Hurr, the commander who first blocked Husayn's road, whose horses Husayn had watered. He asks if there is any repentance for him, and fights at Husayn's side. Then, through the day, the companions fall one by one. Then the young men of the family: sons, nephews, brothers. Tradition counts seventy-two in all who died with him. And at the last, Husayn himself, thirsty, is killed. The women and children are taken captive, among them his sister Zaynab, and his son Ali, who was too sick to fight. Sunni and Shia Muslims both honor Husayn. Sunni Muslims honor him as the Prophet's grandson, and Sunni practice keeps the Ashura fast from the Prophet's own example. For Shia Muslims, Husayn is the third Imam, and the tenth is the center of the year's mourning: gatherings, elegies, tears, the story told again so that it is never told for the last time. The Qur'an speaks to those who fall in God's way. In Pickthall's translation: "And call not those who are slain in the way of Allah 'dead.' Nay, they are living, only ye perceive not." Shia tradition reads Karbala in the light of that verse. One date carries two memories, a people rescued and a family falling, and both are kept.

segments.voice: There's nothing to fix in this one. Let the names you heard come and go, al-Hurr, al-Abbas, Zaynab, Husayn, and keep them company a while, the way people sit with a family after a death. If you pray, you can say, as the Qur'an teaches, we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning; if you don't, just keep the quiet.
Ashura. The tenth day of Muharram: the day the Prophet fasted for Moses' rescue, and the day Husayn and his companions were killed at Karbala. Today's word.
Your line: the tenth day. Rest gently with it, and with all of them. Until tomorrow.

892.title: Zaynab's voice
892.hook: Husayn's sister Zaynab speaks with courage before Yazid in Damascus
892.howItsDone: Shia Muslims retell Zaynab's words in Kufa and Damascus in Muharram gatherings, and her shrine near Damascus is a place of pilgrimage; Sunni Muslims honor her as the Prophet's granddaughter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashura, a day of rescue that also became a day of grief at Karbala. Your line was the tenth day.

A captive is not expected to speak. She is expected to walk where she is led and to keep her eyes down. This captive had just lost her brothers, her sons and her nephews, and she was being marched from Iraq to Syria. She was Zaynab, daughter of Ali and Fatima, granddaughter of the Prophet, peace be upon him. And when she was brought before the men who held her, she did not stay silent.
screen: `A CAPTIVE ON THE ROAD.` → `BROUGHT BEFORE HER CAPTORS.` → `SHE DID NOT STAY SILENT.`

segments.voice: The first time is in Kufa, before the governor, Ibn Ziyad. The histories say he ordered Husayn's sick son, Ali, to be killed, and Zaynab threw her arms around her nephew: if you kill him, kill me with him. The governor let the boy live. Shia accounts add an exchange repeated to this day. The governor mocks her: how do you see what God has done to your brother? She answers: I saw nothing but beauty. Those who tell it hear in her answer that the fallen had chosen their path, and God had honored them. Then Damascus, and the court of Yazid. Al-Tabari tells of a man in the court who asked Yazid to give him one of the captive girls, and the girl clung to Zaynab in terror. Zaynab told him to his face that he had no right to her, and neither did his master. Yazid, angry, said he could do it if he wished. She answered that he could not, unless he left the religion. The girl was not handed over. A collection of speeches by the writer Ibn Tayfur records a sermon she gave in that court, quoting the Qur'an back at the man on the throne: that evil is the end of those who do evil. Shia Muslims honor Zaynab as the voice of Karbala, who carried its story out of captivity so it could not be buried. Sunni Muslims honor her as the Prophet's granddaughter, a woman of patience and strength. Her courage has a particular shape. She did not raise an army. She held a boy, shielded a girl, and spoke.

893.title: The one who prostrates
893.hook: Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who survived Karbala, leaves prayers gathered in al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya
893.howItsDone: Shia Muslims read the supplications of al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the prayers of the fourth Imam, privately and in gatherings, often on particular days and occasions the prayers themselves name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zaynab's voice, a captive who shielded her nephew in Kufa and spoke before Yazid in Damascus. Your line was Zaynab spoke.

The boy Zaynab shielded in Kufa lived. He was Ali, Husayn's son, too sick on the day of Karbala to fight, and he grew into a man who went back to Medina. He did not raise an army. He did not make speeches against the palace in Damascus. What people remembered about him was quieter and stranger: how often, and how long, he lay with his forehead on the ground. They gave him names for it. Zayn al-Abidin, the ornament of the worshippers. And al-Sajjad.
screen: `THE BOY WHO LIVED.` → `NO ARMY, NO SPEECHES.` → `HIS FOREHEAD ON THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Al-Sajjad is tied to sujud, the prostration of prayer, when the forehead touches the ground. Tradition explains the name as one who does it again and again: the one of prostrations. For Shia Muslims, Ali Zayn al-Abidin is the fourth Imam. Sunni scholars honored him too; the hadith scholar al-Zuhri, who knew him in Medina, is reported to have praised him warmly. He left a book of prayers, al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the pages of al-Sajjad, treasured in Shia tradition as words of an Imam addressed to God. The range is wide. Prayers for the morning and the evening, for the new moon, for the coming of Ramadan. A prayer for his parents, asking that he might be gentle with them and lower his voice before them. A prayer for his children. A prayer for his neighbors and friends, asking for the grace to visit the sick among them, to give without being asked, to cover their faults. Even a prayer for the soldiers guarding the frontiers. A man who had lost his father and brothers at Karbala prays for ordinary people's kitchens and doorsteps. Tradition adds a story told about him by Sunni and Shia writers alike. Families in Medina found sacks of bread at their doors by night and never knew from whom. When he died, the bread stopped, and those who washed his body found marks on his back from carrying it. Whatever grief he carried, he turned it into prostration, and into bread.

segments.voice: Take what his prayer for neighbors asks and hold it: visit the sick, give before being asked, cover a fault instead of exposing it. Bring one neighbor to mind, and ask which of those three you might offer them. If you pray, you can bow your head, or put your forehead to the ground.

894.title: Muhammad al-Baqir and Ja'far al-Sadiq
894.hook: Imams of learning in Medina, whose circles, reports say, included Abu Hanifa and Malik
894.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims follow Ja'fari law, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq, and honor al-Baqir and al-Sadiq as the fifth and sixth Imams; Sunni scholars cite reports that pass through them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Sajjad, the one who prostrates, who survived Karbala and left a book of prayers. Your line was the one of prostrations.

A courtyard in Medina. Students sit on the ground in a ring, some with ink and paper, some just listening hard. Questions about prayer, about inheritance, about what a verse means and what a hadith allows. At the center sits a descendant of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Among those who came to circles like this, the reports say, were two men whose names would later be given to whole schools of Sunni law: Abu Hanifa and Malik. The teachers were a father and son, the son and grandson of Ali Zayn al-Abidin.
screen: `A RING OF STUDENTS IN MEDINA.` → `ABU HANIFA AND MALIK, REPORTS SAY.` → `A FATHER AND A SON.`

segments.voice: Start with the father, Muhammad, son of Ali Zayn al-Abidin. He is known as al-Baqir. Tradition explains the title as baqir al-ilm, the one who splits knowledge open. A report kept in Shia sources, and in some Sunni ones, says the Prophet told his companion Jabir that he would live to meet a descendant named Muhammad who would split knowledge open, and asked Jabir to give him greetings. The reports say Jabir did, as an old man. For Shia Muslims, al-Baqir is the fifth Imam. Then the son, Ja'far, called al-Sadiq, the truthful. For Shia Muslims he is the sixth Imam, and Twelver Shia law is still called Ja'fari law, after him. But his circle was wide. Sunni hadith collections, including Sahih Muslim, carry reports that pass through him. Abu Hanifa is reported to have learned from him, and Malik is reported to have said that he never saw anyone better than Ja'far in knowledge and devotion. One more thread, as the reports tell it: Ja'far's mother descended from Abu Bakr, and Ja'far is reported to have said that Abu Bakr was his ancestor twice over. So in one Medina courtyard sit threads that Sunni and Shia Muslims would later follow in different directions, and both still honor the teacher at its center. These two did not answer Karbala with swords. They answered with a school. The splitting-open of knowledge.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Baqir and his son Ja'far al-Sadiq, a father and son teaching in a Medina courtyard. Your line was the splitting-open of knowledge.

A family tree has a way of forking. Two brothers, two inheritances, two sets of cousins who each tell the story from their own branch. The Shia line of Imams forked too, more than once, and the forks have names. Outsiders sometimes call them by numbers: Twelvers, Seveners, Fivers. Those nicknames are rough, and the communities have their own names for themselves. But the numbers open a question Shia Muslims had to answer more than once: when an Imam dies, which son carries the line?
screen: `A FAMILY TREE FORKS.` → `TWELVERS, SEVENERS, FIVERS.` → `WHICH SON CARRIES THE LINE?`

segments.voice: All three tell their story back through Ali and Fatima, Hasan and Husayn. The first fork comes after Husayn's son Ali Zayn al-Abidin, al-Sajjad. One of his sons, Zayd, rose up in Kufa against the Umayyads and was killed. Those who held that an Imam is any descendant of Hasan or Husayn who stands up openly against injustice followed Zayd's example. They are the Zaydis, and because Zayd comes fifth when the line is counted from Ali, outsiders call them Fivers. Zaydi communities live in Yemen today. Others held that the line had already passed from Zayn al-Abidin to Zayd's brother, Muhammad al-Baqir, and then to Ja'far al-Sadiq. The second fork comes after Ja'far. Some held that the line passed through his son Isma'il and Isma'il's son. They are the Isma'ilis, sometimes called Seveners. Isma'ili communities today have their own branches, and some follow a living Imam, present in the world now. Others followed Ja'far's son Musa, called al-Kazim, the one who holds back his anger, and the line went on, father to son, to a twelfth Imam. These are the Twelvers, the Ithna Ashariyya, the Shia of Iran, Iraq, Lebanon and beyond, whose law, as yesterday said, is called Ja'fari. Each line holds that it kept faith with the Prophet's family, peace be upon him. Each has its own scholars, its own prayers, its own sense of what an Imam is. None of them is a footnote to another. Three lines of imams.

896.title: The awaited Imam
896.hook: Twelver Shia hold that the twelfth Imam, al-Mahdi, is in occultation and will return
896.howItsDone: Twelver Shia Muslims hold that the twelfth Imam is alive in occultation; they ask God to hasten his reappearance, and the fifteenth of Sha'ban, remembered as his birthday, is a night of celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: twelve, seven, five. A line of Imams that forked into Zaydis, Isma'ilis and Twelvers. Your line was three lines of imams.

In some homes, when a certain name is spoken, people stand, or put a hand on their heart, and say a short phrase asking God to hasten his coming. The name is the Mahdi, the rightly guided one. For Twelver Shia Muslims he is not a figure from a book of prophecies only. He is a person, the twelfth Imam, the son of the eleventh, alive and hidden, and they await his return. The awaited Imam.
screen: `A NAME, AND PEOPLE STAND.` → `THE RIGHTLY GUIDED ONE.` → `ALIVE, HIDDEN, COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Twelver Shia teaching says this. The eleventh Imam, Hasan al-Askari, had a son, Muhammad. When his father died, the boy was withdrawn from the world by God's will, into what is called the ghaybah, the occultation, the hiddenness. For a time, a few trusted deputies carried his word to the believers; this is called the lesser occultation. Then the last deputy died, and the greater occultation began, which Twelvers hold continues today. The Imam is alive, they say, aware of the world, unseen, and at a time only God knows he will appear, and Jesus will return with him, and together they will set the world right. The word that keeps coming back is justice. A hadith in the collection of Abu Dawud says that even if only a single day of the world remained, God would lengthen it until He sent a man from the Prophet's family, peace be upon him, who would fill the earth with fairness and justice as it had been filled with oppression. Sunni Muslims know that hadith too. In Sunni teaching that accepts these reports, the Mahdi is someone still to come, not the hidden twelfth Imam. So both hope, in different shapes. For Twelvers the hope is very near: an Imam already here, waiting, and believers who try to live as though he might arrive tomorrow. A week that began with a river cut off, after so much injustice, closes on a waiting.
screen: `THE SON OF THE ELEVENTH IMAM.` · `GHAYBAH: THE HIDDENNESS.` · `HE WILL FILL THE EARTH WITH JUSTICE.` · `SUNNI TEACHING: STILL TO COME.` · then, large: `AWAITING JUSTICE.`
